facts.text: On this date in 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 — the first artificial satellite. It orbited Earth every 96 minutes and could be tracked by amateur radio operators worldwide.
On October 4th, 1830, Belgium declared independence from the Netherlands, making it one of Europe's youngest nations despite now hosting the de facto capital of the EU.
More people live inside a circle drawn around Dhaka, Bangladesh than in the entire United States west of the Mississippi River.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined — roughly 60% of the world's total freshwater lakes sit within its borders.
Vatican City issues its own euro coins, but mints so few that collectors buy them at many times face value. The country has no ATMs and its entire economy fits inside a single city block.

On this day in 1987, the Dow Jones fell 91 points — a tremor most traders shrugged off. Thirteen days later, Black Monday erased 22% of the market in a single session, still the largest one-day percentage crash in history.
On October 4, 1957, Sputnik launched — and within days, defense stocks surged while airlines tumbled, as investors briefly priced in the possibility that the Soviets controlled the sky.
The entire US Treasury market, the deepest financial market on earth, went briefly unbuyable for 12 minutes on October 15, 2014. No crash, no crisis — it just froze, and regulators still debate why.

Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway originally made textiles. He bought it as a cigar-butt trade and later called it the worst investment of his life, estimating the mistake cost him $200 billion in compounded opportunity.

The Dutch East India Company, history's first publicly traded corporation, was so dominant at its peak that its inflation-adjusted market cap exceeded $8 trillion — larger than Apple, Microsoft, and Saudi Aramco combined.
On this date in 1957, Sputnik 1 launched — and its radio beep was deliberately pitched so amateur ham operators worldwide could confirm it with cheap equipment. Openness was the point.
On this date in 2004, SpaceShipOne claimed the Ansari X Prize, becoming the first private craft to reach space twice in two weeks. The entire program cost less than a single Space Shuttle launch.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its matter would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Your body replaces the lining of your small intestine every two to four days. The organ doing most of your digestion is essentially never more than a week old.
Light takes eight minutes to reach Earth from the Sun, but nearly 100,000 years to travel from the Sun's core to its surface — trapped, bouncing between plasma particles the whole way.
On this day in 1957, Sputnik entered orbit. It beeped overhead while Eisenhower was playing golf, and engineers at Bell Labs heard it on equipment originally built to study thunderstorms.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Europe's oldest university predates the civilization Cortés would later destroy.
On this day in 1883, the Orient Express made its first run from Paris toward Constantinople — a train ride that outlasted four empires, two world wars, and the currencies of a dozen nations.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She was separated from Khufu by 2,500 years; from Armstrong by only 2,000.
The fax machine was patented in 1843, before the American Civil War, before the telephone, before the light bulb. Japan was still using it as a primary business tool in 2010.
Sonder (n.): the realization that every passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Too precise to stay obscure for long.

Mamihlapinatapai: a Yaghan word for the look shared between two people who both want something but neither will initiate. Yaghan, spoken in Tierra del Fuego, is nearly extinct — one fluent speaker remained as of 2020.
On this date in 1582, October 4 was directly followed by October 15 in Catholic countries adopting the Gregorian calendar. Ten days simply ceased to exist — a bureaucratic deletion from history.

Apricity (n.): the warmth of sunlight in winter. An English word from 1623, coined by Henry Cockeram, that fell out of use entirely — not because the feeling disappeared, but because no one bothered to keep it.

On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, and the word 'satellite' — from Latin satelles, meaning attendant or bodyguard — permanently shifted from describing courtiers to objects in orbit.

On this date in 2013, the FBI seized Silk Road and arrested Ross Ulbricht, confiscating ~144,000 BTC — coins that the U.S. government later auctioned off in tranches, inadvertently timing some sales near local market bottoms.
On this date in 2021, Compound Finance's price oracle briefly reported DAI at $1.30 due to a Coinbase Pro liquidity gap, triggering ~$80M in erroneous liquidations before governance could react.

Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named by Satoshi Nakamoto — the community coined the term in 2010, roughly 18 months after the whitepaper, when micropayment discussions made a subunit name necessary.

Ethereum's gas limit is set by miners and validators through vote, not hardcoded — each block producer can nudge it ±0.1% per block, meaning the limit drifts by emergent consensus rather than protocol decree.

The 2016 DAO hack didn't involve breaking Solidity's logic — the attacker exploited a reentrancy pattern that was already documented as dangerous in Ethereum's own wiki before the contract was deployed.
On this date in 1957, Sputnik launched — and the resulting US panic directly funded ARPA, which by 1960 was financing the first neural network hardware experiments that seeded modern AI research.
Today in 2015, AlexTurner's OpenAI incorporation papers were filed, making October 4th the quiet birthday of the lab that would later train GPT-4 on roughly 25,000 A100s running for months.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have cost over $100 million — yet the model cannot reliably count the letters in a word, because it never sees characters, only tokens.

The transformer architecture, now the backbone of nearly every frontier AI system, was introduced in a 2017 paper by eight Google authors — six of whom have since left Google to found competing AI companies.
Backpropagation was described in a 1974 PhD thesis by Paul Werbos, then ignored for a decade. The algorithm now executes trillions of times per second across global data centers.
